title: Devlens Explainer: What the ICJ ruling can and cannot change for the Rohingya
excerpt: The world court's verdict is binding and final, but it cannot feed the camps or send anyone home. Key questions answered for Bangladesh, donors and NGOs in Cox's Bazar.

image.alt: The Great Hall of Justice in the Peace Palace, The Hague, seat of the ICJ
image.credit: Lybil BER / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

content:
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) gives its judgment today in The Gambia's genocide case against Myanmar. Read our lead story on the verdict day and Dhaka's call for accountability. This explainer sets out what the case is about, what the court can order, and what the ruling can and cannot change for the Rohingya, for Bangladesh and for the agencies and NGOs working in Cox's Bazar and Bhasan Char.

The short answer: the ruling can change the politics around the Rohingya. On its own, it will not change the money, the camps or the timetable for return.

What is the case about?

The Gambia filed the case in November 2019, with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, under the Genocide Convention. It concerns the 2017 military operations that drove more than 700,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh. The Gambia asks the court to find that Myanmar breached the convention, including by committing genocide, conspiring to commit it, failing to prevent it and failing to put suspects on trial.

It is a case between two states about state responsibility. No individual can be convicted in it.

What is The Gambia asking for?

According to a Human Rights Watch (HRW) summary of the case, The Gambia wants:

  • Genocide laws in Myanmar and trials of alleged perpetrators
  • Reparations, including safe return, property restitution, family reunification and protection of the Rohingya's right to identify as Rohingya
  • Compensation or other forms of satisfaction where full reparation is not possible
  • Assurances that the crimes will not be repeated, and a finding that Myanmar ignored the court's January 2020 provisional measures

What does Myanmar say?

Myanmar says its 2017 operations had no genocidal intent and that the evidence is weak. It has filed 12 reports on its compliance with the 2020 order. The Gambia says those reports give "no reason to conclude" that Myanmar complied.

Is the ruling binding?

Yes. The judgment is final, with no appeal, and legally binding on both parties under Article 59 of the court's statute and Article 94(1) of the UN Charter.

Who enforces it?

This is the weak point. If Myanmar does not comply, The Gambia can go to the UN Security Council, which may recommend or decide measures under Article 94(2). HRW notes that the council has never used that power. Kelley Currie, the UN Special Rapporteur on Myanmar, said in Dhaka on 18 November that China and Russia shield Myanmar at the council, The Daily Star reported.

So a finding against Myanmar would mostly work through pressure:

  • From the UN General Assembly
  • From the 11 countries that joined the case as interveners: Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Maldives, Slovenia, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Belgium and Ireland
  • From parallel cases. The International Criminal Court prosecutor asked for an arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing in November 2024, and a court in Argentina issued warrants for 25 people, including him, in February 2025

Will the ruling let the Rohingya go home?

Not soon. Dhaka's position is clear: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said on 18 November that accountability is "essential to delivering justice" and that repatriation is "the only viable and durable solution", The Business Standard reported, citing UNB.

But no one in a position to make return happen expects it quickly. The Refugee Relief and Repatriation Commissioner told The Daily Star that repatriation "will not happen immediately as a direct consequence of the judgment". Thomas Kean of the International Crisis Group told Al Jazeera that the Arakan Army, which controls much of Rakhine State, "can hardly make guarantees around safety while a war is going on".

Refugees want both justice and a way home. "We want to go back," Mohammad Zubair of the Arakan Rohingya Society for Peace and Human Rights told Al Jazeera. A ruling that names what happened to them, and orders reparations that include safe return and restitution, would give them and Bangladesh a stronger legal basis in any future talks. It does not create the conditions for return.

Will it bring more money for the response?

Not directly. The response is already running on less:

  • The 2026 Joint Response Plan seeks $710.5 million for 1.56 million refugees and host community members, 26% less than the 2025 appeal, UNHCR told The Daily Star.
  • Since April, the World Food Programme (WFP) has paid most refugees less than the old flat $12 a person a month. The Refugee Relief and Repatriation Commissioner, Mohammed Mizanur Rahman, said this tiered system is funded only until April 2027. WFP warned in September that general food assistance could be interrupted from December 2026 without more money.
  • Acute malnutrition among children aged 6 to 59 months reached 14.6% in the 2026 Nutrition SMART Survey, up from 8.6% in 2024 and 13.9% in 2025, according to UNHCR figures cited by the paper.
  • HRW said on 16 November that donor-funded programmes enrol 312,000 of about 500,000 school-age children, and that donors had pledged $36 million of a $53 million request for 2026 by mid-October.

Currie said cuts to protection, education and livelihoods are pushing people towards drugs, trafficking and armed group recruitment, and that gender-based violence and serious crimes against children are rising.

A judgment cannot pay for rations, but it may move donor attention, and the timing matters: governments are setting their 2027 humanitarian budgets now. A finding of genocide would make it harder for donors to treat the Rohingya as a lower priority. A narrower ruling could let attention drift further.

What should NGOs do now?

  • Prepare for questions in the camps. Refugees plan to watch the verdict together, and many will hope it means early return. Community engagement and protection teams should be ready to explain plainly what the court can and cannot do.
  • Watch for tension and risk. Currie warned of the risk of renewed violence in Myanmar. A strong verdict could raise expectations; a weak one could deepen frustration. Both can affect safety in the camps and new arrivals at the border.
  • Use the moment for funding advocacy. The case for 2027 pledges for food, nutrition, education and protection is easier to make while the world is watching. National NGOs, which deliver much of the frontline work, have a strong claim to direct funding.
  • Keep host communities in view. Cox's Bazar residents carry much of the cost of the response, and their support will matter in whatever comes next.

What to watch after the verdict

  • The wording of the judgment, especially on genocidal intent and reparations
  • Myanmar's response
  • Whether The Gambia or others take the ruling to the Security Council
  • Donor statements at the end of the year, and whether the verdict shows up in 2027 funding for the Joint Response Plan

Devlens will report the ruling once it is delivered. For today's developments, see our lead story: ICJ rules on Rohingya genocide today as Dhaka seeks accountability.
